steps.why: The sac gathers tears from both lids before they drain down.

steps.label: Nasolacrimal duct
steps.text: The nasolacrimal duct carries them down through the nasolacrimal canal.
steps.why: The duct runs down inside the bony canal of the skull toward the nose.

steps.label: Into the nose
steps.text: The tears empty into the nose below the lowest nasal concha.
steps.why: This last step is why crying gives you a runny nose, and why an eye drop can leave a taste in your throat.

distractors.text: The tears drain straight into the nasolacrimal duct from the surface of the eye.
distractors.why: Tears first enter the puncta and run through the canaliculi into the sac; the duct begins below the sac.

distractors.text: Lacrimal ducts carry them back into the lacrimal gland.
distractors.why: The ducts carry tears out of the gland onto the eye. Nothing returns tears to the gland.

error.text: They drain into openings at the outer corner of each lid.
error.why: The lacrimal puncta sit at the inner corner, near the nose, where blinking delivers the tears.

pathways.summary: Lacrimal gland, lacrimal ducts, across the eye, lacrimal puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac, nasolacrimal duct, nose. Tears are made at the upper outer corner and drain at the inner corner.

pathways.title: Phototransduction in a rod
pathways.intro: A rod sits in the dark, depolarized and releasing glutamate. Then a single photon arrives. Trace how light changes the rod’s signal.

steps.label: Retinal absorbs a photon
steps.text: Retinal in a rhodopsin molecule absorbs a photon.
steps.why: Light acts at only one step: the absorption by retinal.

steps.label: 11-cis to all-trans
steps.text: The kink in retinal straightens: 11-cis-retinal becomes all-trans-retinal.
steps.why: This photoisomerization is the only step that needs light; everything after it is chemistry.

steps.label: Rhodopsin becomes active
steps.text: The opsin changes shape, and rhodopsin becomes active.
steps.why: The shape change of retinal forces a shape change in the opsin around it.

steps.label: Transducin switched on
steps.text: Active rhodopsin switches on many molecules of the G protein transducin.
steps.why: Opsin is a G protein–coupled receptor protein, and one active rhodopsin activates dozens of transducins: the first amplification.

steps.label: Enzyme breaks down cGMP
steps.text: Transducin switches on an enzyme that breaks down cGMP.
steps.why: Each enzyme destroys many cGMP molecules: the second amplification.

steps.label: Cation channels close
steps.text: With less cGMP, the cation channels close, and the dark current stops.
steps.why: cGMP was holding those channels open; as it falls, they shut.

steps.label: Rod hyperpolarizes
steps.text: K+ still leaks out, so the rod hyperpolarizes from about −40 mV toward −70 mV.
steps.why: With Na+ no longer coming in, the outward K+ leak pulls the voltage down.

steps.label: Less glutamate released
steps.text: The hyperpolarized rod releases less glutamate onto its bipolar cells.
steps.why: Release depends on depolarization, so the signal of light is a drop in glutamate.

steps.label: Bipolar, ganglion cells act
steps.text: The bipolar cells respond to the change, and the ganglion cells change their firing.
steps.why: The change in glutamate is the message passed on toward the brain.

distractors.text: Active rhodopsin opens sodium channels directly, and the rod depolarizes.
distractors.why: Rhodopsin acts through a G protein, and light closes channels. The rod hyperpolarizes in light.

distractors.text: Active rhodopsin triggers action potentials in the rod’s axon.
distractors.why: Rods make no action potentials. They signal with graded changes in voltage and glutamate release.

error.text: cGMP rises and opens more cation channels, and the rod depolarizes.
error.why: Light lowers cGMP. The channels close, the dark current stops and the rod hyperpolarizes, the reverse of most sensory receptors.

pathways.summary: Light straightens retinal, rhodopsin activates transducin, and an enzyme destroys cGMP. The cGMP-held channels close, the dark current stops, the rod hyperpolarizes and its glutamate release falls. Two amplifying steps let one photon matter.

pathways.title: Focusing on something near
pathways.intro: You look up at a distant tree, then down at a text message on your phone. Trace how the lens changes shape to focus the near image.

steps.label: Near light spreads out
steps.text: Light from the nearby phone arrives spreading out, so it needs more bending than light from the tree.
steps.why: The problem to be solved comes first: a near object’s rays diverge.

steps.label: Oculomotor nerve fires
steps.text: Parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve fire.
steps.why: The near response is driven by the oculomotor nerve.

steps.label: Ciliary muscle contracts
steps.text: The ring of the ciliary muscle contracts, becomes smaller and moves in toward the lens.
steps.why: Because the ciliary muscle is a ring, contracting shrinks it.

steps.label: Zonule fibers go slack
steps.text: The zonule fibers that hold the lens go slack.
steps.why: With the ring closer to the lens, its threads no longer pull on the lens rim.

steps.label: Lens rounds up
steps.text: Released from tension, the elastic lens bulges into a rounder shape.
steps.why: The lens rounds up by its own elasticity when nothing stretches it.

steps.label: More bending
steps.text: The rounder lens bends light more.
steps.why: A more curved surface bends light more strongly.

steps.label: Image falls on the retina
steps.text: The near image comes to a focus on the retina, and the text is sharp.
steps.why: The extra bending brings the diverging rays together on the retina instead of behind it.

distractors.text: The zonule fibers tighten and squeeze the lens rounder.
distractors.why: Tight zonule fibers stretch the lens thin and flat. The lens rounds up when they go slack.

distractors.text: The cornea changes shape to add the bending.
distractors.why: The cornea’s power is fixed. Only the lens can change its bending.

error.text: The ciliary muscle relaxes, and the ring widens away from the lens.
error.why: That is the state for far vision. For near vision the ciliary muscle contracts and the ring shrinks toward the lens.

pathways.summary: For near vision the oculomotor nerve contracts the ciliary muscle, the zonule fibers go slack, and the elastic lens rounds up and bends light more. With age the lens stiffens and no longer rounds up: presbyopia.

pathways.title: Sound through the ear to the cortex
pathways.intro: A friend calls your name from across the room. Trace the sound from the air to your auditory cortex.

steps.label: Auricle funnels sound
steps.text: The auricle collects the sound waves and funnels them into the ear canal.
steps.why: The external ear is the entrance, and its folds help tell whether a sound is above or below you.

steps.label: Tympanic membrane vibrates
steps.text: The pressure waves vibrate the tympanic membrane at the end of the canal.
steps.why: The eardrum seals the canal from the middle ear and moves with the waves.

steps.label: Ossicles carry it across
steps.text: The malleus, incus and stapes carry the vibration across the middle ear, raising its pressure about 20-fold.
steps.why: The large eardrum and the lever of the ossicles concentrate the force onto the small oval window.

steps.label: Stapes rocks oval window
steps.text: The stapes rocks in the oval window and sets up pressure waves in the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
steps.why: The oval window is where the air-borne vibration becomes a fluid wave.

steps.label: Basilar membrane vibrates
steps.text: The waves make the basilar membrane vibrate most at the place tuned to each frequency, while the round window bulges out.
steps.why: Fluid cannot be compressed, so each inward push of the stapes is matched at the round window, and the wave peaks at its own place.

steps.label: Stereocilia bend
steps.text: The tectorial membrane slides across the hair cells, bending their stereocilia back and forth.
steps.why: The hair cells ride on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane. The outer hair cells' tallest stereocilia are embedded in it; the inner hair cells' are bent by the fluid it drags.

steps.label: Hair cells release glutamate
steps.text: Channels open and close with each bend, and the hair cells release glutamate in rhythm with the sound.
steps.why: Bending opens mechanically gated channels, and K+ entering from endolymph depolarizes the cell.

steps.label: Cochlear nerve fires
steps.text: Sensory neurons with cell bodies in the spiral ganglion fire, in the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
steps.why: The hair cell has no axon, so its sensory neuron carries the signal to the brain.

steps.label: Cochlear nuclei
steps.text: The axons synapse in the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem, on the same side.
steps.why: The first relay is on the same side as the ear.

steps.label: Superior olivary nuclei
steps.text: Signals from both ears meet in the superior olivary nuclei, which compare timing and loudness.
steps.why: This is the first place the two ears are compared, which is how you locate the sound.

steps.label: Inferior colliculus
steps.text: The signal climbs to the inferior colliculus of the midbrain.
steps.why: The inferior colliculus also turns your head toward a sudden sound.

steps.label: Medial geniculate nucleus
steps.text: It relays in the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
steps.why: Hearing, like vision and touch, relays in the thalamus.

steps.label: Primary auditory cortex
steps.text: It reaches the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe, and you hear your name.
steps.why: The cortex keeps the cochlea’s map of frequency, from low notes to high.

distractors.text: The stapes pushes on the round window, setting up pressure waves in the perilymph of the scala tympani.
distractors.why: The stapes sits in the oval window, which opens into the scala vestibuli. The round window at the end of the scala tympani bulges out to relieve the pressure.

distractors.text: The malleus reaches through the oval window and vibrates the hair cells of the spiral organ directly.
distractors.why: The ossicles never touch the hair cells. They move the fluid through the oval window, and the fluid moves the basilar membrane.

error.text: It relays in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
error.why: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay. Hearing relays in its medial neighbor, the medial geniculate nucleus.

pathways.summary: Air, bone, then fluid: the eardrum and ossicles deliver sound to the oval window, the basilar membrane sorts it by pitch, and bent stereocilia make hair cells release glutamate. The signal climbs through the cochlear nuclei, superior olives, inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus to the temporal lobe, reaching both hemispheres from each ear.

pathways.title: How a hair cell turns a bend into a signal
pathways.intro: A sound pushes the basilar membrane upward, and the stereocilia of an inner hair cell bend toward their tallest member. Trace how that bend becomes a burst of action potentials.

steps.label: Bundle bends to the tallest
steps.text: The stereocilia bend toward the tallest stereocilium.
steps.why: The stimulus is a tiny deflection of the staircase-shaped bundle.

steps.label: Tip links stretch
steps.text: The tip links joining each stereocilium to its taller neighbor are stretched.
steps.why: Bending toward the tall side pulls the short tips away from their neighbors.

steps.label: Channels open
steps.text: The mechanically gated channels at the ends of the tip links open.
steps.why: Each tip link tugs its channel open, like a string on a trapdoor.

steps.label: K+ flows in
steps.text: K+ flows into the cell from the K+-rich endolymph around the stereocilia.
steps.why: Endolymph is high in K+ and about 80 mV positive, so both gradients push K+ into the cell.

steps.label: Hair cell depolarizes
steps.text: The hair cell depolarizes.
steps.why: Positive charge entering makes the inside less negative.

steps.label: Calcium channels open
steps.text: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the base of the cell open, and Ca2+ enters.
steps.why: The depolarization spreads to the base, where the synapse is.

steps.label: More glutamate released
steps.text: Calcium triggers the release of more glutamate onto the sensory neuron.
steps.why: As at any chemical synapse, calcium entry triggers exocytosis of transmitter.

steps.label: Sensory neuron fires faster
steps.text: The cochlear sensory neuron fires faster than its resting rate.
steps.why: Because some channels are open at rest, the neuron has a background rate that can rise for one direction of bending and fall for the other.

distractors.text: K+ flows out of the cell into the endolymph, as in most cells.
distractors.why: Around the stereocilia the gradient is reversed: endolymph is K+-rich and positive, so K+ flows in and depolarizes the cell.

distractors.text: Na+ from the perilymph rushes in through voltage-gated sodium channels.
distractors.why: The stereocilia stand in endolymph, which is low in Na+. The current through the tip-link channels is carried mainly by K+.

error.text: The hair cell fires an action potential down its own axon to the brainstem.
error.why: A hair cell has no axon. It releases glutamate onto a sensory neuron, and that neuron carries the action potentials.

pathways.summary: Bending toward the tallest stereocilium stretches the tip links, opens channels, and lets K+ flow in from the endolymph. The cell depolarizes, Ca2+ enters at its base, more glutamate is released, and the sensory neuron fires faster. Bending the other way does the reverse.

pathways.title: Sympathetic pathway: spinal cord to effector
pathways.intro: You are nervous before an exam, and sweat breaks out on your palms. Trace the sympathetic signal from the spinal cord to a sweat gland in your palm.

steps.label: Lateral horn neuron fires
steps.text: A preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of an upper thoracic segment fires.
steps.why: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit only in the lateral horn of T1–L2.

steps.label: Out the ventral root
steps.text: Its axon leaves the cord through the ventral root.
steps.why: Like all motor output, preganglionic axons leave through the ventral root.

steps.label: Into the spinal nerve
steps.text: It enters the spinal nerve for about a centimeter.
steps.why: The ventral root joins the dorsal root to form the spinal nerve just outside the cord.

steps.label: White ramus communicans
steps.text: It turns off into the white ramus communicans.
steps.why: The white ramus is the connecting branch into the chain, white because its preganglionic fibers are myelinated.

steps.label: Synapse in a chain ganglion
steps.text: It enters the sympathetic chain, climbs to a higher level, and synapses on a postganglionic neuron in a chain ganglion.
steps.why: The skin’s supply relays in the chain, and climbing the chain lets upper thoracic outflow reach the arm’s spinal nerves.

steps.label: Gray ramus communicans
steps.text: The unmyelinated postganglionic axon returns to a spinal nerve through a gray ramus communicans.
steps.why: Gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back out; every spinal nerve has one.

steps.label: Out along the arm’s nerves
steps.text: It rides out in the nerves of the arm to the skin of the palm.
steps.why: Postganglionic fibers travel with the spinal nerves to the skin and limbs.

steps.label: Sweat gland secretes
steps.text: Its varicosities release transmitter onto the sweat gland, which secretes sweat.
steps.why: The effector is a gland in the skin, reached only by sympathetic fibers.

distractors.text: It turns off into the gray ramus communicans.
distractors.why: Gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back out of the chain. Myelinated preganglionic fibers enter through the white ramus.

distractors.text: It runs through the dorsal root ganglion into the chain.
distractors.why: The dorsal root carries only sensory axons in. Preganglionic axons leave by the ventral root and reach the chain through the white ramus.

error.text: It passes through the chain without synapsing and runs in a splanchnic nerve to the celiac ganglion.
error.why: That is the route to the abdominal organs. Fibers for the skin synapse in the chain ganglia and return to the spinal nerves.

pathways.summary: Lateral horn, ventral root, spinal nerve, white ramus, chain ganglion (synapse), gray ramus, spinal nerve, effector. Two neurons, with the ganglion near the cord: a short preganglionic fiber and a long postganglionic one.

pathways.title: Sympathetic pathway through the adrenal medulla
pathways.intro: A car swerves toward you, and within seconds epinephrine pours into your blood. Trace the sympathetic route that releases it.

steps.label: Lateral horn neuron fires
steps.text: A preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of a lower thoracic segment fires.
steps.why: Every sympathetic route starts with a preganglionic neuron in the lateral horn of T1–L2.

steps.label: Ventral root and white ramus
steps.text: Its axon leaves through the ventral root and enters the chain through the white ramus communicans.
steps.why: Preganglionic fibers reach the chain through the white rami.

steps.label: Through the chain, no synapse
steps.text: It passes through the chain ganglion without synapsing.
steps.why: Fibers bound for the abdomen do not relay in the chain.

steps.label: Splanchnic nerve
steps.text: It runs in a splanchnic nerve toward the celiac ganglion.
steps.why: Splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic fibers from the chain to the abdomen.

steps.label: Through the celiac ganglion
steps.text: It passes through the celiac ganglion without synapsing.
steps.why: Unlike most fibers arriving there, these have no second neuron to meet.

steps.label: Onto chromaffin cells
steps.text: It ends on chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla and releases acetylcholine onto them.
steps.why: The chromaffin cells take the place of postganglionic neurons: same embryonic origin, but no axons.

steps.label: Epinephrine into the blood
steps.text: The chromaffin cells release epinephrine (about 80%) and norepinephrine into the blood.
steps.why: Without axons, the cells release their product into the blood, as an endocrine gland does.

steps.label: Reaches the whole body
steps.text: Epinephrine circulates to cells all over the body, including cells no sympathetic fiber touches, for a few minutes.
steps.why: As a hormone it reaches every tissue, and it lasts minutes after the nerve signal stops.

distractors.text: It synapses in the celiac ganglion on a postganglionic neuron whose axon reaches the adrenal medulla.
distractors.why: The adrenal medulla is the exception: preganglionic fibers reach it directly, with no postganglionic neuron.

distractors.text: It synapses in the chain ganglion, and a gray ramus carries the signal to the adrenal gland.
distractors.why: Gray rami return fibers to the spinal nerves for the skin and limbs. The adrenal route passes through the chain without synapsing.

error.text: The chromaffin cells send axons to the heart and release norepinephrine onto it.
error.why: Chromaffin cells have no axons. They release epinephrine and some norepinephrine into the blood, which carries them everywhere.

pathways.summary: Lateral horn, ventral root, white ramus, through the chain, splanchnic nerve, through the celiac ganglion, chromaffin cells, epinephrine into the blood. One neuron only: the adrenal medulla behaves like a sympathetic ganglion that secretes into the blood.

pathways.title: The pupillary light reflex as an autonomic reflex
pathways.intro: A doctor shines a penlight into your right eye, and both pupils narrow within a second. Trace the autonomic reflex arc.

steps.label: Retinal ganglion cells fire
steps.text: Light strikes the right retina, and retinal ganglion cells fire.
steps.why: The sensory side starts in the retina.

steps.label: Optic nerve
steps.text: Signals travel along the right optic nerve.
steps.why: The afferent pathway is the optic nerve.

steps.label: Pretectal nuclei, both sides
steps.text: They reach the pretectal nuclei of the midbrain on both sides.
steps.why: The midbrain is the integration center, and it shares the signal with both sides.

steps.label: Edinger–Westphal nuclei
steps.text: Each pretectal nucleus signals the parasympathetic nucleus of the oculomotor nerve (the Edinger–Westphal nucleus) on both sides.
steps.why: These nuclei hold the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the eye.

steps.label: Preganglionic fibers in III
steps.text: Preganglionic fibers run in both oculomotor nerves to the ciliary ganglia.
steps.why: The efferent side is the two-neuron chain; the preganglionic fiber is long.

steps.label: Short postganglionic fibers
steps.text: Short postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins of the circular iris muscle.
steps.why: The terminal ganglion sits right behind the eye, so the postganglionic fibers are short.

steps.label: Both pupils narrow
steps.text: The circular muscle contracts, and both pupils narrow.
steps.why: The effector responds, and less light reaches each retina.

distractors.text: Preganglionic fibers leave the cord at T1 and climb the sympathetic chain to the eye.
distractors.why: That sympathetic route drives the dilator muscle, which widens the pupil in dim light.

distractors.text: Motor neurons in the facial nerve carry the command to the iris.
distractors.why: The facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to glands, not to the eye. The pupil’s narrowing travels in the oculomotor nerve.

error.text: Short postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptor proteins of the circular iris muscle.
error.why: Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons are cholinergic and act on muscarinic receptor proteins. Norepinephrine on alpha-1 contracts the dilator, which widens the pupil.

pathways.summary: Retina, optic nerve, pretectal nuclei, Edinger–Westphal nuclei, oculomotor nerves, ciliary ganglia, circular muscle. Because the midbrain sends the signal to both sides, one lit eye narrows both pupils, and one test checks the optic nerve, the midbrain and the oculomotor nerve.
